topic.title: Setting up and solving quadratic equations by factorising
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One item most series, and often the last question. The usual shape is 'Factorise' for 2 marks and then 'Hence solve' for 2 (Summer 2023 M3 Q21, M4 Q10); the harder shape is a 'show that' setup worth 4 marks with the solve worth 2 (Summer 2024 M3 Q28, where only a handful set up the equation and part (b) was often blank).
mustMemorise: Rearrange so one side is 0, factorise, set each bracket to 0 — and give BOTH solutions
A product is zero only if one of its factors is zero
Never divide both sides by x: that throws away the solution x = 0
Reject a root only when the context forbids it, and write the reason
'Show that' means a forward chain to the printed line, never a substitution
onFormulaSheet: The quadratic formula is printed on the Higher sheet, but this statement asks for a solution by factors
notOnThisSpec: Quadratics that do not factorise over the integers — those need the quadratic formula, which is M4
ax² + bx + c with a not equal to 1 and no numerical common factor (M4)
Completing the square, and solving by graph, are not part of this statement

note.title: Solving quadratic equations by factorising
note.subject: maths

given: Quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a — printed on the Higher sheet, but not the method this statement asks for
mustKnow: A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero
Pythagoras' theorem, for the rectangle-with-a-diagonal setups

notOnThisSpec: Quadratics that do not factorise over the integers — those need the quadratic formula, which is M4
ax² + bx + c with a not equal to 1 and no numerical common factor (M4)
Completing the square, and solving by graph, are not part of this statement

mustBeAbleTo: Solve an equation that is already factorised, such as (x + 4)(x − 6) = 0
Rearrange a quadratic so that one side is zero, then factorise and solve
Solve an equation with no constant term by taking out a common factor, keeping the root x = 0
Solve a quadratic that is a difference of two squares, giving both roots
Use 'hence': carry the factorisation from part (a) into part (b)
Set up a quadratic from an area, from consecutive numbers, from a described number, or from a rectangle with a given diagonal
Answer a 'show that' by a forward chain to the printed line
Reject a root when the context forbids it, and say why in words
Answer in the letter the question uses, and answer what was asked (a length, not x)
sheet.howExamined: M3 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks), and again without a calculator in M7 Paper 1. It is usually one of the last two questions. The common pair is 'Factorise' [2] then 'Hence solve' [2]; the harder version is a 'show that' worth 4 marks from an area or a Pythagoras setup, with a 2-mark solve afterwards. Schemes give M1 for the factorisation or the setup, then an accuracy mark per root, so a single correct root still scores.
traps: Not connecting part (b) to part (a): 'very, very few saw the link', with a single value found by trial (Summer 2023 M3 Q21)
Giving only one solution, usually the positive one (Summer 2023 M4 Q10, Summer 2025 M4 Q10)
Dividing both sides by x, which loses the root x = 0 (Summer 2025 M4 Q10)
Rearranging a quadratic as if it were linear (Summer 2025 M4 Q10)
Solving the printed equation instead of setting it up in a 'show that' (Summer 2024 M3 Q28), or substituting a value to 'verify' it
Muddled signs when reading the roots out of the brackets (November 2025 M3 Q28)
Writing the brackets or the roots in x when the question uses another letter (November 2025 M3 Q28, M4 Q13)
Giving x when the question asked for a length or a base

steps.working: It is already in the form $= 0$, so factorise: two numbers multiplying to $-24$ and adding to 5 are $+8$ and $-3$.
steps.decision: A quadratic can only be solved by factors once one side is zero. Here it already is, so the first move is the factorisation.
Keep the $= 0$ on the line. It is the whole reason the factorisation is useful.
Two numbers multiply to zero only if at least one of them **is** zero. That is the step the factorising was for, and it is what splits the problem into two easy ones.

options: Because a product can only be zero when one of its factors is zero
Because both brackets must be zero at the same time
Because zero divided by a bracket is zero
whyMenu.explain: If neither bracket were zero, their product would be some non-zero number.

steps.decision: Two brackets, two solutions. Both go on the answer line: reporting only the positive one is the single most reported loss on this topic.

steps.working: Rearrange to make one side zero: $x^2 - 9x = 0$.
steps.decision: Never divide both sides by $x$. It looks tidy and it destroys a solution, because $x$ might be zero and dividing by zero is not allowed.

options: Dividing by $x$ assumes $x$ is not zero, and here $x = 0$ is one of the answers
Dividing by $x$ is fine because $x$ cancels
Dividing by $x$ gives $x = 9$, which is the only solution
whyMenu.explain: Substituting $x = 0$ into the original gives $0 = 0$, so it genuinely is a solution.

steps.decision: With no constant term the factorisation is a common factor, not two full brackets. It is still a product equal to zero, which is all that matters.
The first 'bracket' is the single $x$. It is a factor like any other, so it gives a solution like any other.
Check both: $0^2 = 9 \times 0$ is true, and $81 = 81$ is true. Two solutions, both correct.

workedExamples.stem:
A rectangular vegetable bed is $x$ metres wide and $(x + 3)$ metres long. Its area is 40 m².

Form an equation in $x$ and solve it for the width of the bed.

steps.decision: Area is length times width. Writing the equation before expanding anything is a mark in its own right.
Expand, then move everything to one side so that the other side is zero. The factorising method needs that zero.
Two numbers multiplying to $-40$ and adding to 3 are $+8$ and $-5$. Both roots are written down before either is discussed.

steps.working: $x = -8$ is rejected because a width cannot be negative, so the bed is 5 m wide.
steps.decision: The rejection needs a **reason** in words. Simply omitting the negative root looks like forgetting it; saying why it is impossible is what earns the mark and shows the context has been understood.

options: Because a length cannot be negative, so $x = -8$ has no meaning here
Because negative answers are never allowed in algebra
Because the larger root is always the answer
whyMenu.explain: The root $-8$ satisfies the equation perfectly well; it is the context, not the algebra, that rules it out.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The bed is 5 m wide (and 8 m long, giving an area of 40 m²)

A rectangle has a diagonal of 25 cm. Its height is $x$ cm and its width is $(31 - x)$ cm.

Show that $x^2 - 31x + 168 = 0$, and hence find the two possible heights.

steps.working: The diagonal makes a right-angled triangle with the two sides, so $x^2 + (31 - x)^2 = 25^2$.
steps.decision: A rectangle with its diagonal is a Pythagoras question in disguise. Spotting that is the first mark, and it is the step examiners report as missing.
$(31 - x)^2$ is a squared bracket, so it has three terms: $961 - 62x + x^2$. Squaring each term separately would lose the middle one.

whyMenu.explain: Squaring a bracket means multiplying it by itself, which gives four products and a middle term of $-62x$.

steps.decision: Collect, move everything to one side, then divide through by the common factor 2 to reach the printed line exactly.

Two numbers multiplying to 168 and adding to 31 are 7 and 24. Both are valid here: a $7 \times 24$ rectangle and a $24 \times 7$ rectangle are the same rectangle seen two ways, and $7^2 + 24^2 = 625$.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $x = 7$ or $x = 24$ (the rectangle is 7 cm by 24 cm)

twin.stem: A rectangle has a diagonal of 13 cm. Its height is $x$ cm and its width is $(17 - x)$ cm. Show that $x^2 - 17x + 60 = 0$ and find the two possible heights.

options.feedback: Each bracket set to zero in turn. A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero.
The signs were copied straight from the brackets. $x + 4 = 0$ gives $x = -4$, not $+4$.
Two brackets give two solutions. Summer 2023 M4 Q10 reported many candidates writing only the positive root.

items.skill: Solve a quadratic already equal to zero

options.feedback: $(x - 3)(x - 7) = 0$: two numbers multiplying to 21 and adding to 10, both negative.
The brackets are $(x - 3)$ and $(x - 7)$, so setting them to zero gives positive values.
The numbers from the equation were copied out. They are the product and the sum of the two solutions, not the solutions themselves.
Rearranged to $x(x - 7) = 0$. The single $x$ is a factor, so $x = 0$ is a genuine solution: $0^2 = 7 \times 0$.
Both sides were divided by $x$, which quietly assumes $x$ is not zero and throws a solution away.
That would solve $x^2 = 49$. Here the right-hand side is $7x$, so the equation rearranges to $x^2 - 7x = 0$.

items.stem: Part (a) asked you to factorise $x^2 + 5x - 24$. Part (b) says 'Hence solve $x^2 + 5x - 24 = 0$'. What does 'hence' tell you?

options.text: Use your factorisation from (a): set each bracket to zero
options.feedback: 'Hence' means the earlier result is the route. Summer 2023 M3 Q21 reported that very few saw the link.

options.text: Start again with trial and improvement
options.feedback: Trial earns no method marks, and the answer is already half-written in part (a).
It would give the right roots, but 'hence' asks for the factorising route, and this statement is about solving by factors.

items.skill: Take out a common factor first

options.feedback: $2(x^2 - 9) = 0$, so $2(x + 3)(x - 3) = 0$ and the two brackets give $\pm 3$. The 2 cannot be zero, so it contributes nothing.
A difference of two squares always gives a pair. $(-3)^2 = 9$ as well, so $-3$ works too.
The 2 was divided out but the square root was not taken: $x^2 = 9$ gives $x = \pm 3$.

items.stem: A rectangle is $x$ m wide and $(x + 3)$ m long with area 40 m². Solving gives $x = 5$ or $x = -8$. What goes on the answer line?
items.skill: Reject a root with a reason

options.text: 5, because a width cannot be negative
options.feedback: The reason is part of the answer. Stating it shows the context was understood and it is what the scheme rewards.
Both satisfy the equation, but a width of −8 m has no meaning. The context rules one out.
The value is right and most of the marks are safe, but the mark for rejecting the negative root asks for the reason in words.

items.skill: Use the letter in the question

options.feedback: $(c - 5)(c - 6) = 0$. The equation is in $c$, so the answer is in $c$.
The values are right but the letter changed. November 2025 M3 Q28 and M4 Q13 both reported a mark lost for switching to $x$.
The brackets are $(c - 5)$ and $(c - 6)$, so the solutions are positive.

items.stem: A question says 'Show that $x^2 - 31x + 168 = 0$'. What must your working do?

options.text: Start from the information given and reach that line, with every step visible
options.feedback: A forward chain. The printed line is the destination, never a starting point.

options.text: Substitute $x = 7$ and check it gives zero
options.feedback: That verifies one root; it does not show where the equation comes from, and it earns nothing.

options.text: Solve the equation and give both roots
options.feedback: Solving is usually the next part. Summer 2024 M3 Q28 reported many candidates skipping the setup and solving the printed equation instead.

hints: A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero.
Set each bracket equal to zero in turn.

commonErrors.feedback: The signs were copied from the brackets. Solving $x + 4 = 0$ means subtracting 4, which gives $x = -4$.

context.setting: Pure algebra, equations already equal to zero, non-calculator friendly

hints: Two numbers multiplying to 21 and adding to 10, both negative.

commonErrors.feedback: Only one root was given. Two brackets always produce two solutions, and each carries its own accuracy mark.

hints: Opposite signs, because the constant is negative.

commonErrors.feedback: The negative root was dropped. There is no context here to rule it out, so both values belong on the answer line.

context.setting: Pure algebra, the standard factorise-then-solve pair

commonErrors.feedback: That expands to $x^2 - 2x - 35$. The middle term is $+2x$, so the larger number, 7, is the positive one.

scheme.for: their brackets each set equal to zero

commonErrors.feedback: Trial and improvement earns no method marks. Part (a) has already done the work; 'hence' is the instruction to use it.
Only the positive root was written. Summer 2023 M4 Q10 reported this directly: many who made the link still gave one root.

context.setting: Pure algebra, rearranging to equal zero first

hints: One side has to be zero before factorising helps.

commonErrors.feedback: The terms were moved about as if the equation were linear. A quadratic is solved by getting zero on one side and factorising, not by isolating $x$.
The negative root was left out. With no context to rule it out, both solutions are needed.

scheme.for: rearranged to x² − 9x = 0 (not divided by x)

hints: Move everything to one side rather than dividing by $x$.
Both terms share a factor of $x$.
The single $x$ is a factor, so it gives a solution too.

commonErrors.feedback: Dividing both sides by $x$ assumes $x$ is not zero, and it quietly removes the solution $x = 0$. Rearrange to zero instead and take the common factor out.

hints: $x^2 - 9$ is a difference of two squares.
A square root has two values.
parts.workedSolution: $2(x^2 - 9) = 0$, so $2(x + 3)(x - 3) = 0$ and $x = 3$ or $x = -3$. The factor 2 can never be zero, so it gives no solution.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the positive square root was taken. $(-3)^2 = 9$ as well, so $-3$ is equally a solution.

context.setting: Pure algebra, letters other than x

scheme.examinerNote: Answers given as x = 5, x = 6 lose one accuracy mark.

commonErrors.feedback: The values are right but the letter is not. Both November 2025 papers reported a mark lost for switching to $x$ when the question used another letter.
$(y - 6) = 0$ gives $y = +6$. Adding 6 to both sides is the step that fixes the sign.

parts.stem:
A rectangular vegetable bed is $x$ metres wide and $(x + 3)$ metres long. Its area is 40 m².

**Form an equation** in $x$ and solve it to find the width of the bed. Give a reason for rejecting any solution you do not use.

scheme.for: x = 5 chosen, with the reason that a width cannot be negative

hints: Expand and move everything to one side.
One root cannot be a width — say why.
parts.workedSolution:
$x(x + 3) = 40$, so $x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0$ and $(x + 8)(x - 5) = 0$, giving $x = -8$ or $x = 5$.
A width cannot be negative, so $x = -8$ is rejected and the bed is 5 m wide. Check: $5 \times 8 = 40 \text{ m}^2$.

commonErrors.feedback: $-8$ does satisfy the equation, but a bed cannot be $-8$ m wide. The final mark is for choosing 5 and saying why the other root is impossible.
That comes from $2x + 2(x + 3) = 40$, which is the perimeter. The question gives an area, so the sides are multiplied.

questions.solutionProgram: x(x+3) = 40 -> x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0 -> (x+8)(x-5) = 0 -> x = -8 or 5; reject -8 (a width cannot be negative); check 5 x 8 = 40

context.setting: Two consecutive whole numbers with a given product

parts.stem:
Two consecutive **positive** whole numbers have a product of 156.

Form a quadratic equation, solve it, and give both numbers.

scheme.for: 12 and 13, with n = −13 rejected as not positive

hints: Call the smaller number $n$; the next one is $n + 1$.
$13 \times 12 = 156$, so the numbers in the brackets are 13 and 12.
parts.workedSolution:
$n(n + 1) = 156$, so $n^2 + n - 156 = 0$ and $(n + 13)(n - 12) = 0$, giving $n = -13$ or $n = 12$.
The numbers must be positive, so $n = 12$ and the pair is 12 and 13. Check: $12 \times 13 = 156$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $156 \div 2$, which is what you would get by treating the numbers as equal. Consecutive means they differ by 1, so the product is $n(n + 1)$.

questions.solutionProgram: n(n+1) = 156 -> n^2 + n - 156 = 0 -> (n+13)(n-12) = 0 -> n = -13 or 12; 12 x 13 = 156 and (-13) x (-12) = 156 so both are valid for whole numbers, but positive integers give 12 and 13

context.setting: A triangular flag with algebraic base and height

parts.stem:
A triangular flag has base $(x + 4)$ cm and perpendicular height $(x - 1)$ cm. Its area is 18 cm².

Form an equation in $x$ and solve it to find the base of the flag.

scheme.for: base = 9 cm, with x = −8 rejected because a length cannot be negative

hints: Multiply both sides by 2 to clear the half.
The question asks for the base, not for $x$.
parts.workedSolution:
$\tfrac{1}{2}(x + 4)(x - 1) = 18$, so $(x + 4)(x - 1) = 36$ and $x^2 + 3x - 4 = 36$, giving $x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0$.
$(x + 8)(x - 5) = 0$, so $x = -8$ or $x = 5$. A length cannot be negative, so $x = 5$ and the base is $5 + 4 = 9$ cm. Check: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 4 = 18 \text{ cm}^2$.

commonErrors.feedback: $x = 5$ is correct, and four of the five marks are safe. The question asks for the **base**, which is $x + 4 = 9$ cm.

The halving was left out, so the equation became $(x + 4)(x - 1) = 18$, that is $x^2 + 3x - 22 = 0$. That will not factorise, which is itself the warning: a triangle is half of the rectangle around it, so the 18 has to be doubled to 36 first.

questions.solutionProgram: (1/2)(x+4)(x-1) = 18 -> (x+4)(x-1) = 36 -> x^2 + 3x - 4 = 36 -> x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0 -> (x+8)(x-5) = 0 -> x = 5 (reject -8, a length cannot be negative); check base 9, height 4, area 18

context.setting: Pure algebra, a number described in words

parts.stem:
The square of a number is 27 more than six times the number.

Form a quadratic equation and solve it to find the two possible numbers.
hints: 'The square of a number' is $x^2$; 'six times the number' is $6x$.
Nothing in the wording rules out a negative number.
parts.workedSolution:
$x^2 = 6x + 27$, so $x^2 - 6x - 27 = 0$ and $(x - 9)(x + 3) = 0$, giving $x = 9$ or $x = -3$.
Check: $81 = 54 + 27$ and $9 = -18 + 27$. Both work, and the question asks for two numbers, so both are kept.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the positive value was given. Here the context is just 'a number', which does not rule out $-3$, and the question asks for two.

parts.stem:
A rectangle has a diagonal of 25 cm. Its height is $x$ cm and its width is $(31 - x)$ cm.

Show that $x^2 - 31x + 168 = 0$.

scheme.examinerNote: Starting from the printed equation, or substituting a root, earns nothing.

hints: The diagonal makes a right-angled triangle with the two sides.
$(31 - x)^2$ has three terms — write it as $(31 - x)(31 - x)$ first.
Collect and take everything to one side.
There is a common factor of 2 to divide out.

commonErrors.feedback: $(31 - x)^2$ was taken as $961 + x^2$, so the $-62x$ never appeared and the equation collapsed to $2x^2 + 336 = 0$, which no value of $x$ satisfies. Squaring a bracket produces a middle term; write it as two brackets first.

parts.stem: Solve the equation to find the two possible heights of the rectangle.
hints: Two numbers multiplying to 168 and adding to 31.
Both roots make sense here: they are the two sides of the same rectangle.
parts.workedSolution: $(x - 7)(x - 24) = 0$, so $x = 7$ or $x = 24$. Both are valid: the rectangle is 7 cm by 24 cm, and $7^2 + 24^2 = 625 = 25^2$.

commonErrors.feedback: Only one root was given. Here neither is impossible — they are the height and the width of the same rectangle — so both belong on the answer line.

parts.stem:
To solve $x^2 = 5x$, Séamus divides both sides by $x$ and writes $x = 5$.

Explain what is wrong with his method, and give the complete solution.

accepted: Dividing by x assumes x is not zero and loses the solution x = 0; the solutions are x = 0 and x = 5

scheme.for: a statement that dividing by x assumes x ≠ 0 and so loses a solution

hints: Put $x = 0$ into the original equation and see whether it works.
What is not allowed when you divide?
Rearranging to zero and taking out a common factor keeps both solutions.
parts.workedSolution:
Putting $x = 0$ into $x^2 = 5x$ gives $0 = 0$, so $x = 0$ is a genuine solution. Dividing both sides by $x$ assumes $x$ is not zero, so that solution is thrown away.
The safe method is to rearrange: $x^2 - 5x = 0$, so $x(x - 5) = 0$ and $x = 0$ or $x = 5$.

commonErrors.feedback: The answer $x = 5$ is one of the two, so the method looks fine until you test $x = 0$. Summer 2025 M4 Q10 reported weaker candidates rearranging a quadratic as if it were linear; the same instinct is at work here.

context.setting: A rectangular garden with a border removed

parts.stem:
A rectangular lawn measures $(x + 7)$ m by $(x + 2)$ m. A square pond of side 3 m is dug out of it. The area of grass remaining is 27 m².

Show that $x^2 + 9x - 22 = 0$.
hints: Lawn area minus pond area equals the grass remaining.
parts.workedSolution:
$(x + 7)(x + 2) - 3^2 = 27$.
Expanding: $x^2 + 9x + 14 - 9 = 27$, that is $x^2 + 9x + 5 = 27$.
Taking 27 across: $x^2 + 9x - 22 = 0$, as required.

commonErrors.feedback: The pond was subtracted as 3 rather than $3^2$. A square of side 3 m has area 9 m².

parts.stem: Solve the equation and hence find the length of the lawn. Give a reason for rejecting the other solution.

scheme.for: x = 2 chosen, with the reason that a length cannot be negative

hints: Two numbers multiplying to $-22$ and adding to 9.
The length asked for is $x + 7$, not $x$.
parts.workedSolution:
$(x + 11)(x - 2) = 0$, so $x = -11$ or $x = 2$.
A length cannot be negative, so $x = -11$ is rejected and $x = 2$. The lawn is $x + 7 = 9$ m long.
Check: the lawn is $9 \times 4 = 36 \text{ m}^2$, the pond is $9 \text{ m}^2$, and $36 - 9 = 27 \text{ m}^2$ of grass.

commonErrors.feedback: A negative value of $x$ would make the width $x + 2$ negative, so it cannot be a length. Test each root against the shape before writing it down.
$x = 2$ is correct, and two of the three marks are safe. The question asks for the length of the lawn, which is $x + 7 = 9$ m.

parts.stem:
A rectangular photograph is $x$ cm wide and $(x + 5)$ cm tall.

It is placed in a frame that adds 2 cm to the width and 2 cm to the height. The framed picture has an area of 176 cm².

Form an equation in $x$ and solve it to find the width of the photograph.

scheme.for: x = 9 chosen, with the reason that a width cannot be negative

hints: The framed width is $x + 2$ and the framed height is $(x + 5) + 2 = x + 7$.
parts.workedSolution:
Framed width $= x + 2$; framed height $= x + 7$.
$(x + 2)(x + 7) = 176$, so $x^2 + 9x + 14 = 176$ and $x^2 + 9x - 162 = 0$.
$(x + 18)(x - 9) = 0$, so $x = -18$ or $x = 9$. A width cannot be negative, so the photograph is 9 cm wide.
Check: framed size $11 \times 16 = 176 \text{ cm}^2$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the framed width, $x + 2$. The question asks for the width of the photograph itself, which is $x$.
$-18$ satisfies the equation but not the picture: a photograph cannot have a negative width. The last mark is for saying so.

findTheMistake.stem: Rónán was asked to solve $x^2 + 3x - 28 = 0$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The numbers were copied straight out of the brackets instead of being solved for. $x + 7 = 0$ means $x = -7$, not $+7$.
correction: x + 7 = 0 gives x = −7; x − 4 = 0 gives x = 4
findTheMistake.feedback: The factorisation is correct and earns the method mark, and the two brackets are correctly set to zero. The last line reverses one sign: solving $x + 7 = 0$ means taking 7 from both sides. A quick substitution catches it — $7^2 + 21 - 28 = 42$, not 0, while $(-7)^2 - 21 - 28 = 0$.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoibhe was asked to solve $x^2 = 6x$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Dividing by $x$ assumes $x$ is not zero. Here $x = 0$ satisfies the equation — $0 = 0$ — so a solution has been thrown away.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two roots is right, so something is salvaged. The habit to build is fixed: a quadratic is rearranged so that one side is zero, and then factorised. Dividing by the unknown is never safe, because the unknown might be the thing that is zero. Summer 2025 M4 Q10 reported weaker candidates rearranging a quadratic as if it were a linear equation, which is the same instinct.

findTheMistake.stem: A rectangular patio is $x$ m wide and $(x + 2)$ m long, with an area of 35 m². Cormac was asked to form an equation and find the width. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Both roots solve the equation, but only one can be a width. A patio cannot be $-7$ m wide, so that root has to be rejected — and the rejection needs a reason in words.
correction: A width cannot be negative, so x = −7 is rejected
The patio is 5 m wide (and 7 m long, giving 35 m²)
findTheMistake.feedback: Four of the five marks are safe: the equation, the rearrangement, the factorisation and both roots are all correct. The last mark is for reading the algebra back into the context and saying which root the situation allows, and why. It is one sentence, and it is a mark every series. The same sentence also guards against the opposite slip, discarding a root that the context does in fact allow.

prompts.prompt: The four steps for solving a quadratic by factorising.
prompts.answer: 1 Rearrange so that one side is zero. 2 Factorise. 3 Set each bracket equal to zero. 4 Give both solutions.

prompts.prompt: Why does setting each bracket to zero work?
prompts.answer: Because a product can only be zero when one of its factors is zero. If neither bracket were zero, their product would be some non-zero number.

prompts.prompt: You have $(x + 8)(x - 3) = 0$. What are the solutions?
prompts.answer: $x = -8$ and $x = 3$. Each bracket is solved, not copied: $x + 8 = 0$ gives $-8$.

prompts.prompt: Why must you never divide both sides of $x^2 = 6x$ by $x$?
prompts.answer: Because it assumes $x$ is not zero, and $x = 0$ is one of the solutions. Rearrange to $x^2 - 6x = 0$ and factorise to $x(x - 6) = 0$ instead.

prompts.prompt: A context question gives the roots 5 and −8. What do you write?
prompts.answer: The value the context allows, with a reason for rejecting the other: 'a length cannot be negative, so $x = 5$'. Silently dropping a root does not earn the mark.

prompts.prompt: 'Hence solve' follows a 'Factorise' part. What does it mean?
prompts.answer: Use the factorisation you have just written. Another method, including trial or the formula, is not the route the scheme rewards here.

prompts.prompt: What must a 'Show that' answer do?
prompts.answer: Start from the information given and reach the printed line, with every step visible. Substituting the answer in, or starting from the printed line, earns nothing.

prompts.prompt: How do you set up a quadratic from a rectangle with a given diagonal?
prompts.answer: The diagonal and the two sides form a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras gives $a^2 + b^2 = d^2$. Expand any squared bracket in full, collect, and take everything to one side.
$961 - 62x + x^2$. Squaring a bracket means multiplying it by itself, so there is always a middle term.

prompts.prompt: Which quadratics are NOT solved by this method?
prompts.answer: Any that will not factorise over the integers, and any where the coefficient of $x^2$ is not 1 and has no common factor. Those need the quadratic formula, which is M4.

findings.asked: Factorise a quadratic, then solve the linked equation.
findings.wentWrong: Factorising was excellent (a few sign mix-ups). The solving part was very poor: most did not connect it with (a), and many who did wrote only the positive root.
findings.rule: Each bracket = 0 gives one solution; report both.

findings.wentWrong: Factorising was right or wrong outright. Very few used it to solve; most offered x = 5 alone, found by trial.
findings.rule: Use your factorised form - it is the method the mark scheme rewards.

findings.asked: Set up a quadratic from the information, then solve it.
findings.wentWrong: Only a handful set up the equation; many just solved the printed one, and some who factorised correctly listed only one solution.
findings.rule: Two brackets, two solutions, both on the answer line.

findings.asked: Factorise (common factor, then difference of two squares), then solve a simple quadratic.
findings.wentWrong: Taking out only 4 instead of 4a scored nothing for the first part. In the solving part weaker candidates rearranged as if the equation were linear, and some dropped the negative root.
findings.rule: A quadratic is solved by factorising or the formula, never by moving terms like a linear equation.

findings.wentWrong: About a third succeeded; many did not see the need for two brackets, signs were muddled (-12c and +27), and some wrote the brackets in x.
findings.rule: Use the letter in the question and check the signs multiply back correctly.

findings.asked: Factorise a quadratic in c, then a difference of two squares.
findings.wentWrong: Well done overall, but using x instead of c cost a mark and any wrong sign cost both.
findings.rule: Same letter as the question; signs must reproduce the middle term.

insight.ruleToRemember: Factorise, set each bracket equal to zero, and give both solutions in the variable the question uses; part (b) almost always uses part (a).
insight.aStarSignal: Choosing factorising over trial when a quadratic appears inside a longer problem, and stating both roots before selecting the one the context needs.
